Header:
Date: 2025-04-11 15:30 UTC | Duration: ~62 min
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Li (Redwood Research), Samir Kapoor (Mercury Pay - Head of ML), Lena Ortiz (Mercury Pay - Platform), Darren Cho (Mercury Pay - CTO)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be rough): Align on consistent benchmark methodology for runtime latency/throughput and configuration effects (KV cache, batching, quantization). Agree to share harness and schedule pilot.

00:00 Alex Chen: okay hey everyone thanks for joining, um so the goal for today is fairly simple - workshop the methodology so both teams run apples to apples benchmarks, sounds good?
00:08 Samir Kapoor: yeah thanks Alex, we really want to understand like tail latency tradeoffs and how kv cache warmup changes numbers, cause in our payments flows a 1% tail increase is bad, so we need reproducible tests
00:20 Maya Patel: totally makes sense, we see that a lot; quick agenda: prompt set, load generation (closed vs open loop), metrics to capture (p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, GPU util, HBM), and config matrix (batch size, kv cache settings, quantization). we'll propose a runbook.
00:35 Darren Cho: quick context, we have an on-prem-ish private cluster in AWS Outpost and want to compare Redwood Private vs our self-hosted Triton experiments. security is a big constraint.
00:50 Jordan Li: just to add, for apples-to-apples we need to standardize tokenization, model weights (same checkpoint), sequence length distribution, and random seeds where applicable. Otherwise fp16 vs int8 numbers become noisy.

02:10 Samir Kapoor: question - when you say kv cache hits, what are you measuring? is it prefix cache or full-kv?
02:16 Maya Patel: good callout; we recommend measuring both: prefix (identical prompt prefixes where you can re-use kv) and live-kv cache that persists between requests. For our benchmarks we report two modes: cold (no cache) and warm (cache hit rate measured). important to surface hit rate as percent and also break down p99 when hit vs miss.

04:05 Lena Ortiz: on load generation, we currently use k6 for HTTP-level load and a small custom client; is closed-loop feasible?
04:12 Maya Patel: yeah there are two modes: closed-loop (client waits for response before sending next) which simulates user latency SLOs, and open-loop (fire at target RPS) which stresses throughput. For inference, closed-loop highlights tail latency behavior under realistic concurrency. Open-loop shows max tokens/sec and throughput ceilings. We suggest both.

06:30 Jordan Li: another gotcha: batching behavior changes with request size distribution. If you have wide variance in prompt lengths, average batch size shrinks and latency improves/worsens unpredictably. So supply a realistic token length histogram with the prompts.
06:50 Samir Kapoor: ok we'll export token length hist from production logs, but we need to be careful about PII.
06:58 Darren Cho: on quantization, we are sensitive to QA degradation. how do you recommend balancing int8 speedups vs accuracy?
07:10 Jordan Li: recommend a 3-stage approach: 1) run synthetic benchmarks fp16 baseline for throughput/latency, 2) run int8 with outlier detection turned on and evaluate on a held-out prompt set for quality regression, and 3) run user acceptance tests. We also provide guidance on per-layer quantization and progressive quantization (first int8 on activations only, then weights). We log sampling outputs and compute perplexity + task-specific metrics.

09:40 Maya Patel: regarding metrics to capture in each run: p50/p90/p95/p99/p999 if possible, mean tokens/sec, GPU utilization (smoothed 30s), GPU memory (HBM), CPU, network egress, cache hit rate, batching distribution (hist of batch sizes), and model throughput in tokens/sec for different sequence lengths. Also capture warm-up curves over time to see cache ramp.

12:02 Samir Kapoor: you mentioned p999 — our infra tooling doesn't export that easily, will p99 be okay?
12:08 Alex Chen: p99 is typical but for payments tail it's good to look at p995/p999; if it's hard, at least include the max observed latency and count of > SLO events.

14:30 Lena Ortiz: on VPC/on-prem specifics, we get noisy network variance and NFS metadata latency - how do you isolate network noise from runtime behavior?
14:45 Maya Patel: isolate by doing local measurements: run the model container and benchmark within the same host first (loopback) to get baseline. Then run across your VPC with synthetic network egress measurements. Use iperf for raw bandwidth and run experiments at low network utilization to establish a baseline, then at target production network util. Record network metrics alongside inference metrics and correlate spikes.

17:00 Jordan Li: for warm vs cold cache tests we recommend 3 phases: 1) cold-run (single-shot requests to prime model, empty cache), 2) cache-warmup run (repeat prefix group to achieve target hit rate), 3) steady-state run (measure after warmup). Record hit-rate per prefix group. Repeat the whole experiment 3 times to get variance.

20:30 Samir Kapoor: ok how many prompts do you usually include in the corpus? we have thousands but want a representative set
20:38 Maya Patel: typical corpus sizes: 200-1000 prompts for iterative experiments; for production-level benchmarking use larger corpora (2k-10k) and stratify by token-length buckets and prompt type. We'll provide a template CSV with fields: prompt_id, prompt_text, avg_tokens, category, expected_output_snippets.

23:10 Darren Cho: on hardware comparability, we want to compare your Redwood Dedicated numbers (NVIDIA H100/RTX?) to our on-prem A10s. How do you ensure fair comparison?
23:25 Jordan Li: the key is to normalize per-token cost and per-GPU theoretical throughput. Use the same model checkpoint, sequence length, batch formation algorithm, and measure tokens/sec per GPU and tokens/sec per-dollar if possible. Also report kernel versions, CUDA/cuDNN, and full env (glibc, container runtime) so results are reproducible. Avoid wall-clock-only comparisons without specing batch shapes.

26:40 Samir Kapoor: vendor-specific kernels (like Triton optimizations) may differ — we should capture that in notes.
26:46 Maya Patel: yes capture runtime stack and kernel caveats. For apples-to-apples we also recommend running on identical driver stacks if possible or at least noting differences.

29:05 Alex Chen: let's talk about load shape — steady RPS vs bursts. For payment workflows we see spiky bursts; we recommend including spike tests (x3 baseline RPS for 60s) and evaluate recovery/backpressure behavior. Also test model fallbacks: can Redwood route to smaller model under high load? we're fine to measure candidate fallback behavior.

31:30 Samir Kapoor: question on instrumentation: is there an open-source collector you recommend for per-token latency?
31:38 Maya Patel: we usually provide a token-logger shim in the harness (instruments response stream events and timestamps per token), plus an aggregator that computes per-token and per-chunk latencies. We also push aggregated metrics to prometheus/grafana. We'll share the shim.

34:10 Jordan Li: note on sampling bias: if you do open-loop and push too much concurrency you saturate GPU memory and get OOM or degraded perf; always include a health probe and backoff policy so you can distinguish saturation from normal latency characteristics.

36:50 Lena Ortiz: about quantization quality checks — how do you compare outputs? exact-match rarely useful, so what metrics?
36:58 Jordan Li: we run a suite: task-specific metrics (e.g., BLEU/ROUGE for generation tasks), embedding similarity (cosine between fp16 baseline embeddings and int8 embeddings), and human sampled evaluation on a small holdout. Also compute distributional stats (logit differences, perplexity). We'll flag regressions above a threshold for review.

40:12 Samir Kapoor: what about the effect of batching on safety / moderation latencies? batching can increase latency for short but frequent requests.
40:22 Maya Patel: true, you need to pick batching policy aligned with SLOs: static batching (fixed batch window) vs dynamic batching (threshold-based) and latency-aware batching (max latency cap). We'll capture both in the matrix and recommend policies per SLO bucket.

43:00 Alex Chen: on the actual runbook: propose a config matrix CSV with rows for each experiment: model, quantization, batch_policy, batch_size_target, load_mode, target_rps/concurrency, sequence_length_bucket, expected_hit_rate. Each run should produce an artifact bundle: raw logs, perf metrics, token-logger, environment.yml, and a summary CSV.

46:15 Samir Kapoor: sounds good. Can you give a quick example experiment?
46:20 Maya Patel: example: model-x-7b, fp16, dynamic batching, target concurrency 16 closed-loop, seq bucket 32 tokens, warm-cache 80% hit rate, run for 10 minutes after warmup. Collect p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec. Repeat 3 times and report median.

48:30 Lena Ortiz: security artifacts — we need SOC2 and encryption at rest details before we allow pilot on our staging.
48:40 Alex Chen: understood, we'll email the SOC2 pkg and KMS integration notes. We'll also provide a short summary of RBAC/SSO options for Redwood Private.

50:12 Samir Kapoor: do you have recommendations on stress tools? we use k6 but you're recommending locust for more granular control?
50:20 Maya Patel: k6 is fine for HTTP-level RPS. For token-level streaming and custom pacing we prefer locust or a custom async client; we provide both examples. The harness supports both open-loop and closed-loop drivers.

53:00 Jordan Li: small note on reproducibility: version-control the exact prompt set used and random seeds for any sampling. For chat-style models freeze system prompts and mention truncation/prefixing behavior.

55:30 Darren Cho: timeline — how quickly can we run the first pilot?
55:37 Maya Patel: if you can provision staging access and share prompt corpus by next week, we can run a pilot within 7-10 days. We'll need the VPC peering toggled and credentials for ingestion.

57:10 Alex Chen: ok recap of next steps: Redwood shares harness + runbook, Mercury Pay shares prompt set and staging access, both align on closed vs open loop targets and SLOs, schedule pilot. Action items recorded.

60:05 Samir Kapoor: thanks everyone, appreciate the depth here — this is helpful.
60:12 Alex Chen: thanks all, we'll follow up by email with links and the SOC2 packet.
